images.caption: Figure 1:OVMI maps incomparable evaluations onto a common scale.Speech BCI studies differ in experimental setting, supported vocabulary, and test data, so their reported scores are not comparable. Each study provides a decoding score over its supported vocabularySS, from which we estimate the information conveyed within that vocabulary,II. We define a common reference distributionp⁡(x)p(x)over the words a user may wish to communicate, and letC⁡(S)C(S)denote the probability that a word fromp⁡(x)p(x)is supported by the system. OVMI weights the decoded informationIIbyC⁡(S)C(S), yielding a score that measures performance againstp⁡(x)p(x). Evaluating all systems against the samep⁡(x)p(x)therefore allows comparing heterogeneous speech BCI studies on a common communication scale.

Figure 5:Speech BCI performance depends on the intended communication domain.Each cell reports OVMI normalised by the entropy of the corresponding reference distribution, as a percentage, with uncertainty beneath. Brackets denote propagated intervals for published invasive results, whereas±\pmdenotes one-SEM uncertainty for Tang and LibriBrain100. Armeni and MEG-MASC are excluded for brevity. Systems are evaluated against four communication references spanning broad spoken English(van Heuven et al., 2014, SUBTLEX-UK;), conversational speech(Godfrey et al., 1992, Switchboard;), augmentative and alternative communication(Erickson et al., 2019, AAC/UCV;), and narrative speech(Doyle, 1892, Sherlock Holmes;).
